review_title: When a Story Becomes a Gift!!
body: ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ (But honestly, 5 stars isn't enough.) I've been an avid reader for many years, and Theo of Golden has earned a place among my all-time favorite books. I went to bed last night knowing I had to log in for work early this morning, but I literally could not stop reading until I finished. And when I turned that final page, I wasn't sure whether my tears were from the story itself or from it being over. It was definitely both. I loved every single second of this book. What I especially loved was that I never had it figured out. IYKYK. I enjoyed the story so much that I was never looking for where it was going, and when the last quarter of the book hit. :::Sigh::: I'm struggling to find the right words because some books are simply too special to summarize. Every so often, as a reader, you come across a story that hits differently, a story that is so heartwarming, beautiful, and meaningful that reading it feels like receiving a gift you didn't even know you needed. Theo of Golden is exactly that, and so much more. I went into this book completely blind. The simplicity of the cover caught my attention, and something about the title just spoke to me. I purchased the Kindle version, but I'll absolutely be ordering the paperback because this is one I need on my bookshelf. I'm not even going to attempt to explain the plot because I don't want to take away from anyone else's experience. What I will say is that I was completely transported into this story. I could vividly picture every place mentioned. The writing was descriptive without ever feeling excessive or slowing the pace, which is something I truly appreciated. There are a lot of characters in this book, a lot of names and stories intertwined. Normally, that can feel overwhelming, but somehow it never did. When Theo met someone, I felt like I met them too. I never struggled to keep track of anyone because every character felt real, distinct, and memorable. Trust me when I say you need to visit Golden. You need to meet Theo. You need to experience the people he encounters along the way. And perhaps most of all, you'll find yourself wishing that every one of us could meet someone in our lives who possesses even a fraction of Theo's kindness, wisdom, and heart. The writing is beautiful, effortless, and flows so naturally that the pages seem to turn themselves. Allen Levi absolutely knocked his debut novel out of the park. This book reminded me why I fell in love with reading in the first place. I will eagerly read anything this author writes next. I can not wait to read this again!!

product_title: Theo of Golden: A Novel
body: This book caught my eye while browsing the staff-recommended selections at a small bookstore. Soon, I began seeing it mentioned as a word-of-mouth sensation on social media. Curious about how a self-published book by an unknown author could have gone viral in today's overcrowded book market and attracted millions of readers, I dove in. The hook and plot are compellingly simple. A mysterious, wealthy octogenarian who calls himself Theo but refuses to reveal a last name or discuss his past moves from New York City to the small Georgia town named Golden, where he ingratiates himself into the community by gifting portraits from a local artist and through other selfless acts of kindness. It's a feel-good tale that showcases the power of human connection, empathy, and goodness. There's a strong Christian element to the story, and it uses the power of art and music in ways that are genuinely moving and uplifting. Although the writing flows well and has a poetic flair at times, the author's choice of third-person omniscient narration for a story in which the big reveals (Theo's true identity and the reason for moving to Golden) are withheld until the end is rather unorthodox. The author's overwhelming preference for telling rather than showing also knocks it down a peg when judged on its literary merits. But the story is deeply touching nonetheless, proof that conforming to literary conventions isn't as important as agents and big publishers seem to believe if an author's work connects this well with its audience.

The main character himself has suffered loss yet maintains his optimism, sees the goodness in those around him, and in his quiet way gives of himself to others. The story carries strong themes of unconditional love for others, family, faith, and shows us how one person can affect those around them with simple words and gestures. While tragedy and violence play a role in the story, there is also hope. Get ready for a surprise ending, deepened by a satisfying resolution. If you like suspense, lots of action and romance this is probably NOT the book for you, but if you enjoy a slow-paced, thoughtful story with multiple point of view characters and back stories that pull at your heartstrings, you will probably enjoy this one.

body: I knew I would love this book instantly. A mysterious old man appears in a town to kindly, sweetly, and beautifully change the lives of every soul he meets. I haven’t finished the book. I’m entering Chapter 51, but I have already decided that this will be a book I read twice. The first time, I feel, I am reading steadily to absorb and complete my understanding of the story from end to end. But the second time will be to “marinate” in the words of the book. I am a devoted and avid gardener. When I began my current garden—a lovely piece of earth my husband and I have created together over many years—it was a very blank canvas. One stroke of the shovel and one handful of dirt led to another and another, until it was molded into a tiny botanical garden of sorts. In it, one surprise and wonder leads to another. The vision of the completed garden was always viewed from what a visitor might see and feel when experiencing it for the first time. That vision all began with a quote from an unknown author that is pinned near my office window that overlooks the garden. It states, “All good garden paths should lead to loitering with fine intent.” This book often leads you to stop and read the words again, or simply pause to marinate in the words themselves. This good book leads to “loitering with fine intent.” To create a story such as this in your head is an incredible thing, but to “put it to paper” is something altogether different. The story itself is touching, and beautifully written, but there are deep, rich layers in the story and in the characters as well that take root in the reader. This book does not qualify to be put in the category of  just “A Good Read,” but rather in that special category of exceptional books that bring you to self-reflection.  It makes you ponder about the people who have crossed your path—not as random encounters, but as people God may have purposefully placed there. It makes you think about how far-reaching thoughtfulness and kindness can be, and how the simplest of things can bring unexpected joy to another person. It may lead you to wonder what more kindness, more thoughtfulness, in your own life would look like. How to be more, give more, love more. This is a book to pursue when you have the time to linger…to loiter with fine intent, with the expectation that it may change you. Its words may whisper to you again and again, well after the final page is turned. To Allen Levi, I hope this is the greatest compliment I can give.

product_title: Theo of Golden: A Novel
body: Theo of Golden is one of the most memorable books I’ve ever read. I’ve never considered myself much of a reader. I often lose interest after starting a book or struggle to remember what I’ve read. This one was different. I couldn’t put it down. Allen Levi has created a character whose quiet strength, compassion, and humanity stayed with me long after I turned the final page. Theo is mysterious and intriguing. His life is marked by deep heartache, yet he chooses to love, serve, and see the beauty in others. His story made me laugh, brought tears to my eyes, and more than once had me ugly crying. What surprised me most was how this book changed me. It didn’t just entertain me—it gave me a fresh perspective on how to live and love well. It left me wanting to be a “Theo” in the lives of the people around me. Few books have moved me this deeply. I sincerely hope this story is someday adapted into a movie or television series so even more people can experience it. I’ll definitely be reading more of Allen Levi’s work. If you’ve been wondering whether to read Theo of Golden, don’t hesitate. It’s a gift.

body: You may find what you bring to the book. Richard Feynman voiced what i imagine every neurologist and psychologist would recognize as important, "humans are emotional, not rational, Human beings are not rational, we rationalize." (Paraphrased as remembered.) In a time of discord in our society's soul, so to speak, a kindness has appeal. As any novel is difficult to write that doesn't have tension, violence, episodic payoffs it is a miracle that this book toward a goodness can hold together. It doesn't for some cynics, objective academics and souls that rightly have discussable issues with it, and like all of us, with themselves. Having read the one star reviews they have discussable points with a third showing emotional responses as well as objectivity. Emotions are valid, but they are our/their own and to be weighted as such. Some of them correctly notice what isn't treated in the story. That is intellectually tricky territory as we are to review what was written. In that vein I'm reminded of professor Walter Kaufman of Princeton Univ circa 1940-1970s(?) who said there are three steps in our search for truth: 1) our narrative, 2) even if we best the opposite in a debate, because we are a better debater, we need to make their argument for them, but 3) even then if we are still right we need to ask ourselves what did he see that he doesn't know he saw, but is of merit for consideration, Here he likened to a jungle native who had never encountered outside civilization nor seen gold, seeing a lost city of El Dorado with castles made of solid gold trying to go back and tell his people what he saw.  (This happened for Pigeon Egg's Head, Native American after visiting DC when he went back to his people who ousted him after his barrel of whiskey ran dry, as the biggest liar on earth.)  He saw something even if he got it wrong. Here I suggest that Allen Levi with his too good for some readers, Theo, emphasizes the - "one an other" that is in religion, but also in any social studies or psychology. He seems to be saying by repeatedly trying to show with words, image is the strongest form of communication and he tries to paint word images of a person both sharing and then listening in depth - to who the person  is. Our society has lost that. We have gone reportedly gone since 2020 in video from needing 12 second dopamine fixes to 8 1/2 now. (I know i like my I phone, internet, whatever next.) (I phones aren't even for talking to people, we don' t even do that and the author takes them out of the story also.) We are in a society that needs its moral, economic and state systems. In politics and high offices there are actions that maximize power by using people as means to a greater end v seeing people as ends in themselves. These can be considered antithetical for our purposes here. Two different ways of being, perhaps threshold matters, perhaps conditions of though precedent. That Theo is not believable to some suggest that a person who exists and who is swilling and invested in finding and listening to other humans deeply is no longer believable as a reality. If so, that is telling. He sees them and in turn leaves the hope that we all can be seen and be seers and be kind. Whether we are existentialists or Christians or atheists , "one another" is huge. If you liked "The Education of Little Tree" 40 years ago, where grandma told Little Tree "the first thing you do when you get something good is find some one to share it with," this book may be for you. The issue the author addresses in his way is bigger than the book, and as big as our civilization, if i may say so. I am thankful he tackled writing about good, which i find very difficult to do. Theo of Golden may be as rare to some's belief as and old order Amish coming into my living room and sitting down to talk, but damn what a story. I am naive enough I was able to suspend believe and be enchanted. At 83, this and Where the Crawdads Sing and a couple of James Lee Burke's description of hurricanes coming in have been it for me for several decades. Read and write, God gave you a mind, eyes and a number two lead pencil. Enjoy. --Jan

product_title: Theo of Golden: A Novel
body: I started this novel on audio 6 days ago as I sat down for my last platelet donation. And despite it being a 120 minute donation, I was completely engrossed in the novel, so much so I didn’t even check to see how much time had passed.  The narration was done by David Morse, and although his female voices are not very distinctive, he was the right person for this book. Despite that, I ended up alternating between listening to the book and reading it myself, depending on what I was doing, and it worked well. The mysterious Theo shows up in the town of Golden, Georgia one day, and introduces himself as Theo. No last name, no other identifying feature. He’s an 87 year old man who treats people with kindness, but prefers to live in anonymity. As it turns out, he confides to one person, but even we don’t know who he is. What we do learn, is the type of person he is or has chosen to be at this time of his life, and he forms a close circle of friends. I loved this novel because I loved the conversations he had, as his gentle inquisitive nature, his ability to read people, and his generous spirit gave people the space to share their stories, often for the first time. We get to learn some of those stories, and as such, we get to know some of his closest friends more than the other people in town. We see how he loves his neighbors and how he allows them to love him back. And how unexpected friendships grow between the people he chose to surround himself with. My only dissatisfaction with this novel is that I wanted to know more about some of these friends of his. I wanted to care more about them, on a visceral level. As much as I loved this story, I just didn’t feel quite as emotionally invested as I would have expected. I teared up a few times, especially towards the end, and perhaps it’s because I was interrupted a few times when I was on the last chapter (before the epilogue), but I should have been sobbing, and I wasn’t.  And while I loved everything that happened in the epilogue, it felt a bit rushed, like the narrator was just telling you everything that happened after Theo’s time in Golden, just so that we would know. And yet, despite this lack, I would still recommend this novel. And yes, I still loved it. It was beautifully written, and I loved the idea of Theo with his beautiful handwriting spending the time to craft wonderful letters to each of the recipients, as well as to his friends. I loved the theme of choosing how you want to live your life, sprinkling daily acts of kindness all around you, big and small, and the ripple effects of those acts. Allen Levi, if this is an accidental novel, I can’t wait to see what you write when you mean to do so. Highly recommended!

review_title: The Magic of Stories, the Wonder of Words
body: This is the third of three books I've read this summer (along with We Burned So Bright and Pure Men) at which I have openly wept while sitting in coffee shops. I'll admit I found the ending a little too neatly wrapped up.  (Still working through that criticism).  But the story is so sweet and life- affirming that I've been recommending it to everyone. The town of Golden with its coffee shops, bookstores, artists, musicians, eccentrics, and gorgeous environment is exactly the kind of town I would love to live in -- come to think of it, I do!  And the title character -- so kind, generous, cultured, elegant, curious, and loving -- is the kind of elderly gentleman I aspire to be. (Underline "aspire").  Some readers have criticized the book for being too sweet, too idealized.  For God's sake! It's a parable, not a documentary, a book that teaches how we can live a fuller, more generous life if we just choose to do so (for the record, I'm choosing to do so.).  I saw that Tom Hanks has bought the rights and will star in the film.  It's too bad that we've lost Fred Rogers. He comes very close to being the embodiment of Theo and would perfect for the role.

product_title: Theo of Golden: A Novel
body: A few weeks ago a pastor mentioned a book during his sermon and I immediately added it to my cart. It has sat there for a few weeks then again I saw someone else recommend the book and I knew it’s what I wanted to take on during our first driving day to the canyon. I just finished reading Theo of Golden, and I’m not quite sure how to explain it except to say it felt like sitting on a porch with a wise friend. Theo is an 86-year-old man who settles in the small town of Golden. He isn’t flashy. He doesn’t set out to change the world. He simply notices people. Have you ever complimented someone’s dress and watched their face light up? Or remembered someone’s favorite flower and surprised them with it months later because you make mental notes of the small things people say and do. There is something deeply human about being seen. We all want to know that we matter. Has someone ever just asked you about your life and then genuinely given you full access to talk without interrupting and truly listening about something you are passionate about, a time In your life you experienced serious grief, or a dream you have for your life. Theo has a way of giving people that gift. He notices. He asks questions. He remembers details. He makes people feel like their story matters. As I read, I couldn’t help but think that perhaps one of the reasons people were drawn to Theo was because he offered something that has become increasingly rare….his attention. One line from the book especially stayed with me: the idea that sometimes people simply need help sitting still long enough to see what is already there. What I found most interesting is that this is a Christian book that doesn’t wear a Christian label. There are no sermons tucked into the chapters. Instead, the faith shines through the way Theo loves people. His life quietly reflects the heart of a brother who has learned that kindness, patience, and attention are often some of the greatest gifts we can give. The book also carries a beautiful truth: sometimes we mend our own broken hearts by helping mend someone else’s. Theo carries his own grief, yet rather than turning inward, he spends his days caring for the people around him. In doing so, he becomes a source of healing—and perhaps finds healing himself. I closed the book wanting to be a lot more like Theo. A little slower. A little more attentive. A little more willing to notice the people God places in front of me each day

review_title: A story of art, music and writing
body: Like the face of heaven. That’s how I see Theo, and I hope this will be a movie. “Theo of Golden” is the debut novel by Allen Levi. He was writing as a personal challenge and just doing some scenes. He began writing in 2019-2020. He had been a songwriter and lawyer. He has no connection to Portugal, which is mentioned in the book quite a bit and led me to try Port wine. This book will lead me to do a lot of things. Theo is a supremely interesting man! More on that other familiar interesting man in a later post. The book will make you want to look at the faces of people. Use a gaze that calms and loves. Be kind and generous. Greet people. Be less fearful and exchange stories. Be attentive. Love people up close. Invest in the art of living. Be beautiful, useful and pleasurable.  All which I should be doing, but will now do for Lent. Theo listened with genuine interest, adoringly, encouraging and with gratitude. Newborns look for their mother’s face, a particular gaze that calms, loves and welcomes them. Someone they recognize, run to greet and someone to bond with. Levi signs the books “With thanks for the Theo in you.” He greets kids at a high school three days a week. He reads to second graders. He doesn’t mind being around people not like him. The coffee shop setting is a real place in Columbus, Ga. It’s called Fountain City Coffee. In picking bestowals of the sketches there, Theo looked for someone lost, weary, worried or troubled that the gift would encourage or help. I got to hear him in a Zoom. A group of women from Vermont who lost their daughters came to Georgia on a pilgrimage. He was a steward of clean rivers and water and said the river still flows after death. He went through a “walking season” in losing his daughter. In a book about knowing a person, it is mentioned that a bench is a good way to do this. 7 p.m. was Theo’s meeting time with the strangers for bestowals and ended up being the time of the funeral. He also mentioned “Think Little” by Wendell Berry. Do so and if everyone does, it spreads. Levi was born in 1956. His dad is 98. His mother passed and he lost his brother, whom he called a clone of Theo, at 55. His dad was a forester, explaining his interest in nature. Springtime is an end with a future, said Theo. One character named Tony runs the Verbivore book store and has the Penny Loafers out there because they haven’t spent a penny and they majored in loafing. Theo and Tony end up having Port together and he told Theo is Viet Nam stories. The Penny Loafers were better than a room full of Senators. They lie. Tony ends up being more of a believer of Jesus at the end because he wasn’t before Theo. James Ponder has no degrees hanging in his office. Note the “ponder” mentions throughout. He is a dispenser of advice, secret keeper and agent of calm. Secretary Mrs. Gidley was suspicious of Theo at first but comes around. Ponder was Theo’s landlord and mentioned the 18-inch railing and three flights of stairs before the 86 year old decided to live there. Kendrick reminds me of the custodian who won “America’s Got Talent,” who has an ill daughter Lamisha, who wants to be a  physical therapist or artist in the end. Her education will be paid for by Theo as were some of her medical bills. Maria Menendez is the daughter of the “little man” who killed Theo’s wife and daughter in an accident. Maria had cancer. I don’t want to give away too much, but Theo decided to love Asher, the sketch artist, with two hearts. And there is much more to that. Simone wears a wardrobe that honors music on stage and guests who come to listen did the same. Cello intricacies became fascinating to me and I looked up some of the music mentioned. His bow was a gift from Theo. He played Fado for Theo at his concert. It ended up being a requiem with three characters, Kendrick and Basil, the busker. Simone’s parents were there and I wasn’t clear if Theo sprang for their trip. At the end, Basil studies to get a doctorate in American literature. Katherine is the reporter who respects Theo’s wishes while many people she interviews are praise seekers and applause junkies. He was a friend, not a headline. Ellen rides a bike and I’ll just call her different. He gave her a foldable handsaw, cordless sander, drill and wood burner to make feather boxes. I have made one because of this book. She had $1,600 to her name from selling them, but gave the money to the cello fund after she and Simone were assaulted and the perpetrator was never caught. Cleave is the poisonous guy—like a snake, hemlock, black widow or “words with no wisdom guy.” All but Cleve show community in sitting on the same row or pew. They all have sparks of hope. I loved this line: We walk all roads, long and winding. Road to ruin. Easy Street. Road less traveled. I’m so mad that my notes from Chapter 10-28 somehow disappeared. I may reread. This post would be longer. I probably have a dozen favorite books and just added this one.

review_title: A parable that makes me proud to be a Georgian Artist
body: I finished this book in 2 days during my Key West 2026 vacation. My friend Ritchie texted me to read it and I downloaded it every day. Author Allen Levi self published Theo of Golden in 2023 before it garnered a national book deal in 2025. As a founder of a regional theatre - this book would make the most wonderful play. Hiring one actor who can draw that during the course of the evening draws one member of the audience. The dreams I dream as I near retirement. I love any book where the artist is Asher. I too, know an amazing artist named Asher. I long to be Theo, a Portuguese artist who travels to rural Georgia to revisit the home of his long lost love. I long to travel to a town, buy art on the wall of a coffee shop and give it to the owner of the face it displays. I read a review from a Good Reads enthusiast who said it didn’t seem plausible to start so many random conversations with strangers, which I do all the time. She was clearly put off that the book felt Christian in nature. Both of these elements drew me to the tale, that Jesus himself might liken to a parable. As someone vacationing with people I met from having a random conversation in Key West and who is strong in her faith - I was unusually moved by the book. Thank you for telling Theo’s story - a story of a man from another land (Portugal) falling in love and being deserted, a story of a the unpredictable Ellen with her magical bike, Tony - a very loud bookstore owner who bemoans his so called failing business (I know the type), Mr. Ponder, a financial advisor with a very nice apartment for Theo to rent, Kendrick - a father and janitor and parent we all aspire to be, Simone a cello player (or my friend Noah) Simone a street musician (or my new friend Scott) and countless other characters that I attached my own friends’ likenesses to. If I do not live another day, I am glad I see the potential in humankind and how it is reflected in a simple likeness in a piece of art. For me it was the perfect book.

review_title: The 2nd best book I’ve ever read…
body: only second to the Bible. There are books that entertain. There are books that inform. And then, on exceedingly rare occasions, there are books that leave you wondering whether you are the same person who closed the back cover as the one who opened the front. Theo of Golden is one of those books. I don’t say this lightly: it is the second-best book I have ever read—second only to the Bible. Not because it rivals Scripture, for nothing can or should, but because no work of fiction has so beautifully illuminated the truths Scripture has already revealed. It is the kind of story that refuses to remain on the page. Long after the final chapter, its themes continue to echo in your mind, exposing your assumptions, enlarging your view of grace, and awakening a deeper awareness of the fingerprints of God in the ordinary moments of life. The genius of Theo of Golden isn’t merely found in its prose or plot—though both are exceptional. Its brilliance lies in its ability to make eternal realities feel startlingly personal. It doesn’t preach at you; it invites you. It doesn’t manipulate emotion; it earns it. And somewhere along the way, without realizing it, you stop reading a novel and begin examining your own soul. Great books give you memorable characters. Extraordinary books give you a new lens through which to see the world. Theo of Golden gave me both. If every library burned to the ground and I could rescue only two books, the first would be my Bible. The second would be Theo of Golden.

review_title: Vincent van Gogh said genuine art is to love people - Theo does that well
body: “But for anything to be good, truly good, there must be love in it…” is my favorite quote from Allen Levi’s book "Theo of Golden" which is one of those rare novels that reflects love on every page. Theo arrives in the small town of Golden, Georgia with nothing but a paintbrush and a heart tuned to see people as God sees them. And somehow, through the simple act of gifting portraits, he helps ordinary folks feel seen, known, and valued. This book reminds us that goodness still exists, that hope can be found in everyday life, and that sadness and joy can coexist without canceling each other out. Reading Theo of Golden will expand your capacity for empathy, restore tenderness, then gently remind you of the kind of love that makes art and life good. In a world obsessed with achievement, noise, and self‑promotion, this quiet, self‑published story became a NYT #1 literary phenomenon the old‑fashioned way — through love, beauty, and word‑of‑mouth wonder. Everyone who reads it tells somebody else - that's how I found it, and now Theo has become one of my favorite novels of all time. Pick it up, give yourself time to sit on the bench with Theo, then get ready to really see the people around you."

body: I have watched hundreds of the greatest films of all times and have a library full of many great books. Even so, I do not often write reviews. Just finished listening to the Audible version of Theo of Golden and I feel the same way about this work as I did after watching or reading (or shall we say “experiencing”) for the first time other great and monumental works of past. I can only imagine the movie that will come from this book assuming it is done justice. This story is a masterpiece and you are richer for having heard it. This is a storylover’s paradise and I am pleased to see that there are still authors who can write this way in our day and age. I believe this may well go down as one of the better novels of our time and I recommend it to anyone with a love of life, art and all things pure and beautiful. My hope is that the enjoyment of what this book embodies will not be a fad that passes as soon as it has begun, but will it be taken to heart, baked into you, and from you permeate the world around wherever you are. Theo’s spirit can be alive in all of us if we let it. May you be fully invested in the “art of living” and engaged in the “conspiracy” of bringing kindness to your corner of the world.

review_title: A Moving, Universal Story That Stays With You
body: Title: A Moving, Universal Story That Stays With You I don’t normally read this kind of fiction, and I have always resisted books we are told we are supposed to "mechanically appreciate" through a forced academic lens. But Theo of Golden completely won me over by letting the story simply flow on its own terms. While the book is rich with literary mechanisms, symbolism, and deep biblical principles, it is far more than a faith-based story. The core themes at play, fairness, genuine kindness, and radical mercy, are not proprietary to any single belief system; they are universal human truths. It balances life's beauty with its harsh, sudden warts in a way that feels deeply authentic. This is an extraordinarily enjoyable read that respects the reader, defies rigid categorization, and leaves you with insights that will marinate in your mind for a very long  time.

Eventually, as I read, I wasn't even sure I'd find the reason why Theo was doing what he did (or even care at that point) but then when least expected the answer came in the most explosive way possible, completely jarring me from a beautiful tale to sorrow that it couldn't just go on and on like a never ending tale. body: More than simply a sweet tale of kindly old man, this story crawls in slow and hits you deep if you let it.  No, it's not action packed, full of high stakes moments, risky behaviors or morally ambiguous characters who make questionable choices.  Also, no, it's not just a cute story about cute people having a really nice day.  It's a deeply moving tale about what really matters in life -- every life -- not just the ones worth reading about.  THEO's strong and gentle message is one we need today, and every day.  I have to note that this novel breaks all of today's rules about novel pacing, stakes, action and character arcs, and it's STILL a viral success, begging the question, why are modern literature and machine that drives it (big publishing houses) obsessed with formulas that might not be working?  Maybe today's readers are teaching the lesson the big five publishers need to learn.  Deliver solid content told humanly, with heart.  Maybe then we can beat the bots.

product_title: Theo of Golden: A Novel
body: A common question: “What is Theo of Golden about?” I can answer that two ways. In summary, it is about a humble, Portuguese man in his 80’s, Theo, who comes to live in the town of Golden, Georgia. He visits a coffee shop with a wall decor of 92 framed portraits and is inspired to connect each pencil drawing with the person represented. He buys a picture, invites the subject of the drawing to a park bench, gifts the depiction, and encourages that person to talk about themselves. That description is accurate, but falls short. Theo of Golden is about kindness, about looking into a person’s eyes to see their soul, about listening to their story, and about walking alongside them in times of pain and of joy. Yes, Theo of Golden is about kindness. Not random acts of kindness, but intentional, well-planned, respectful acts of kindness that are born of love. Theo of Golden can be viewed as a book with Christian themes—or not. Its perspective is that of a man who wants to make the world a better place. I don’t think the author set out to write a “Christian book”; but, as a Christian, he did create a character who lives out the example set by Jesus. Kindness is held to be a positive value, something one should ascribe to, whether viewed as part of the Christian faith or not. Most of the book is a slow and careful revelation of Theo. He is  initially an enigma to the townspeople, but soon they accept him, appreciating casual interactions on a daily basis or a deep friendship with him that develops for some of them. Along the way to learning more about Theo, we meet many of his new friends—a night janitor whose daughter is hospitalized after an accident, a talented graduate student with a passion for the cello, and a homeless lady with mental issues. Tony, the owner of the Verbivore, a bookstore, is perpetually “a week away from closing his doors.” Asher is the prolific artist who created the portraits. Theo, with his quiet, calm, and kind ways, makes a difference in all of their lives and in that of so many of Golden’s residents. Theo of Golden is a book that deserves a re-read as so many details will take on more depth of meaning when the reader has the benefit of a type of omniscience in regards to the characters and the plot. This novel will enchant and inspire; it will bring chuckles and tears. In the end, it will leave no reader unmoved.

review_title: Brilliant Hard Sci-Fi, But Denser Than The Martian – Torn on Book vs. Movie – 4/5 Stars
body: I just finished Project Hail Mary by Andy Weir, and it’s one of the few book-to-film adaptations where I’m genuinely torn on which version I prefer. The book has a more serious, grounded tone overall compared to the movie, which leans a bit more into humor and pacing. Both are excellent in their own ways. As someone who thoroughly enjoyed both the book and the film adaptation of The Martian, I went into this expecting a similar balance of clever science, problem-solving, and witty narration. Weir delivers on the first two in spades—Ryland Grace’s journey to save Earth (and his own skin) is packed with inventive hard sci-fi that feels meticulously researched. However, there were stretches where the scientific explanations became way too dense and technical for my taste. I found myself mentally slogging through some sections, which led to many late nights over the 23 days it took me to finish. That said, the story, characters, and stakes are incredibly compelling, and the payoff is absolutely worth it. It’s smart, hopeful, and emotionally resonant in ways that stuck with me. I’ll probably need a break from heavy science-heavy reads for a little while after this one, but I still highly recommend Project Hail Mary to fans of smart, high-concept sci-fi.

product_title: Project Hail Mary
review_title: Spoiler-free Review - The Martian Dialed Up To 11
body: If you loved the Martian in either book or movie form, Project Hail Mary will likely delight you. The main character (who I'll leave nameless to avoid spoilers) is nearly identical to The Martian's lead, Mark Watney. They have similar personalities, the same fundamental mission of surviving in a hostile environment, and both use real-world biology, chemistry, and physics to solve their problems from start to finish. The book provides an early test for whether or not you'll enjoy it: on page five, when our protagonist is being quizzed by an annoyingly paternalistic computer that is demanding to know the cube root of eight, our hero replies with the smart aleck answer: "two times e to the two-i-pi". If you find this interaction amusing, all good; if it's off-putting, turn back now. In fairness, Project Hail Mary shares The Martian's flaws as well. The protagonist's character is a bit better developed - but only slightly. The conflict is entirely man-vs-environment. And though the protagonist is often in situations that might cause one to ponder the essential truths of the human condition, he never does. His personality and behavior as a sarcastic problem-solving scientist / engineer are pitch-perfect but the book rarely goes any deeper. He has an established motivation and a flaw to be overcome - but these are really just superficial grace-notes (see what I did there?). This is not Crime and Punishment. Instead, it's a page-turning action-hero book - where instead of firing shots, the action hero saves the day by doing science really well. Books that celebrate real science are rare, so if that's what you came for, you're going to love what Project Hail Mary delivers. Although largely similar, there are four main ways in which Project Hail Mary differs on the Martian so I'll touch on those now: 1. The stakes are higher - much higher! In The Martian, Mark Watney is already a bit of a super hero - he's an astronaut after all - and all he really needs to do is stay alive. In Project Hail Mary, our hero is much more of an every-man and his job is nothing less than to save the human race. 2. The Martian is told in chronological order. In Project Hail Mary, our hero awakens with a serious case of amnesia and can't even remember his own name. He starts his adventures at essentially the most dull part of his recent life. As time passes he both tackles dramatic new challenges and remembers the wild adventures that brought him here. Andy Weir does a fantastic job of interweaving the past and the present and the result is a very effective narrative framework that lands on a "Wow!" moment at the end of nearly every chapter. 3. Project Hail Mary is a buddy story. In The Martian, Mark Watney is alone in his battle against the elements of Mars for nearly the entire book. By contrast, Project Hail Mary, once it really gets going, is absolutely a tale of buddy-bonding. This surprised and, ultimately, delighted me. It helps give the protagonist a bit more of a human side. And the team problem-solving scenes are, again, pitch-perfect. 4. Project Hail Mary puts the 'fiction' back in Science Fiction. In The Martian, leaving aside the opening wind storm and the closing chapter of wish-fulfillment heroics, we are essentially in a very tightly written NASA simulation. I found this incredibly enjoyable - but one could reasonably ask, where are the big ideas? Where are the bold 'what ifs'? The answer is, they're in Project Hail Mary! The science is still real and omni-present, but the fiction is big, bold, and awesome. If you're main draw for the Martian was the NASA lore and you wished Weir would write an even tighter sequel detailing the Apollo 13 events, you may be a bit disappointed - but everyone else is going to love this change of pace! So that's it in a nutshell: Project Hail Mary is a fantastic next book to read after The Martian. It's a clear spiritual successor but brings new ideas and structure to the game. Enjoy!

review_title: Proof that lightning strikes twice ... Weir has done it again!
body: According to a 2003 article on the NASA website, "NASA-funded scientists have recently learned that cloud-to-ground lightning frequently strikes the ground in two or more places ..." and that the third and fourth strokes of a lightning flash will follow the same path as the second stroke.  In other words, lightning DOES strike the same place twice. But you don't need to search the web for this information.  If you want proof that lightning strikes twice, just read Andy Weir's newest book, Project Hail Mary, and you'll see that Weir has created a giant sci-fi bestseller, in the same electric path as The Martian. Ryland Grace has a puzzle on his hands.  He wakes up without a clue as to where he is, but he seems to be alone except for a computer AI that was keeping him alive. Unfortunately it didn't seem to be doing the same for two others in his ... wherever he is ... as he notes the decayed corpses in their creches on the ... well, it's a ship.  A space ship. And bit by bit Grace puts the pieces of the puzzle together. An alien microbe has been discovered. Ryland Grace is brought on to the science team to learn more about the life form because Grace, currently a middle school science teacher, wrote papers about the notation that there does not need to be water to create life.  Only in a biozone such as Earth's would water be needed, but other building blocks could be used in other systems. The science community as a whole mocked Grace, which is why he left and went on to teach kids, but now, he may be the best suited to understand this new life form. And as he remembers more and more, he also remembers that this life form is feeding on the energy output of the sun, which is decreasing the energy that gets to Earth, which spells disaster - as in the end of all life as currently known - on Earth if something isn't done. Scientists discover that Sol isn't the only star that is losing its energy output - likely due to the alien consumption, but that there is one star, in the center of all the known stars losing their energy, that remains constant with its output.  In which case, the answer to the survival for Earth is likely found there, at Tau Ceti. The world's best scientific minds come together (by force and coercion) to create a ship that can get to Tau Ceti in twelve years (using the alien microbe as fuel) with shuttle pods to bring back answers to how to save the planet, but for the crew, it's a one-way trip. Knowing why he's there is only the first puzzle for Grace.  Now he has to figure out how to save Earth.  There's a very small window of time for him to discover the way to save the human race and get the answers sent back.  Take too long and the shuttles will return to a dead planet. This book is amazing. Author Andy Weir brings us back to the magic that made The Martian so successful - an abandoned scientist trying to survive.  But Ryland Grace's story is more complicated because he's not just trying to survive, but also help humanity survive. There's lots and lots of science - which is part of Weir's writing signature - and there's also a really wonderful story. It's hard for me to tell you just what I liked about this book because anything I write will be a spoiler and a huge part of the joy in this book is making the discoveries with Ryland Grace. Grace is our main character, but through the liberal use of flashbacks, we have a full cast of characters - at least one quite important to the story. Everyone is unique and individual which makes it easy to read, but just as with The Martian, where Mark Watney's personality carries the story, Ryland Grace here is the smart-mouth, sometimes funny, obsessed scientist infusing his personal tastes into his discoveries. He's also quite smart - which is good since he will need his intellect to save all of humanity. This is a page-turner. I did not want to put this book down. Neither did my 21 year old son who picked up my copy after I was well into it and finished it before I did. And days later he's still talking about how much he liked it and quoting sections of it to me at the dinner table. I hope Ballantine Books will do a very large print run because this is going to be huge seller and you definitely don't want to miss out on the biggest thing to come out in 2021. Looking for a good book? Project Hail Mary by Andy Weir is proof that lightning strikes twice as this has all the excitement and energy of Weir's debut novel, with a more complicated storyline that will hold the reader all the way to the end.

body: This was a book club pick. Honestly, I wouldn't have chosen to read this myself, but I'm glad that I did. I would have missed out on an incredible story. I've been reading a lot of thriller and fantasy books lately, that I forgot how much I enjoy sci-fi. This brought it back for me. There's a lot of science-heavy discussions in the book and I loved it! When I got to a subject or term I didn't know, I would go online and learn more about it. I feel that Grace is a dork like me because he wouldn't curse. He had little anecdotes he uses in place of swearing. Something I definitely do myself! A lot of the book is the MMC talking to himself. Surprisingly, it worked. There's so much humor that it kept the story going. There was not a lull. Usually I dislike info-dumping as an introduction to get all the background story told, but I didn't mind it at all. Maybe I'm being biased because I love science talk. **SPOILERS AHEAD** What makes the whole plot engaging is the fact that the plot doesn't seem too fantastical. It's something that could happen. There's a lot of ethics and morals involved in determining what should be done. I would hate to be in a position where I have to chose what's best for everyone. That's why Stratt is a necessary character. I hated some of her decisions and how she operated, but you need someone who's focused on the general welfare of humanity. I would be too focused on myself, my family, etc. As much as it hurts to admit, I'm selfish (and a coward) like Grace. I wouldn't want to die. But was it right for Stratt to force him on the mission? This could also be taken religiously. If God has a plan and things happen for a reason, is it our right to deter what's going to happen? God wiped out the world many times because of humanity's sins, what if this was God's doing? So many questions and debates on right vs wrong, ethics vs morals, and religion vs humanity made for a incredible book club discussion. I love how this book ended. I wish I could continue reading about Rocky and Grace's adventures, it's that fascinating. However, I think Grace staying on Erid was the best outcome. If the roles were reversed, I don't think Rocky would have the same welcome. I feel that those in charge would have dissected and kept Rocky hostage, all in the name of science. Just as the Astrophage were first introduced, the first things the scientists did was poke and probe. Essentially torturing the Astrophage to see what makes them tick. I think Rocky would have the same fate. Oh, and my favorite part is the relationship between Rocky and Grace. I cried so many times when I was reading. Scared that something bad was going to happen to either of them. Especially in the scene where Rocky busted out of his tunnel to save Grace. I got upset and told the book that 'if Rocky dies, I swear, this is the worst book ever!' And the scene where Rocky learns about radiation poisoning. How he slowly becomes aware of what happened to his crew, his friends. I was a mess. This book is definitely one that I could go back and reread. I did watch the movie afterwards. There's a lot of differences to adapt the story to screen, but it was okay. They got the humor down pat, but I didn't get the direness of the whole situation nor the special bond that both MCs had.

body: With the movie releasing in a week, I had to make sure I read this before I went to go see it, since I didn’t do it with Weir’s last adaptation, The Martian. Project Hail Mary is a phenomenal end of the world, first contact, sci-fi thriller from a first-person pov, that had me from the moment I started it to the final page. Ryland is easily my favorite character so far this year and Rocky comes in at a close second. To be honest, I’m not sure I have a single critique about this book, everything worked perfectly. From the well researched science per the acknowledgements to how it felt very cinematic, as if Weir had written this for the very purpose of an adaptation. I’m not sure where he drew from, but I could see many likely inspirations like Interstellar, Passengers and Ad Astra, where it’s an epic journey into the unknown, racing against time to save the world, and self-discovery with a little bit of humor thrown in. Where this differs from those is the back and forth story-telling of present tense in space and the past filling in gaps of who he is, how he got there and what he did along the way. Doing this opens up the story by adding more characters so it’s not just a quiet, introspective voyage through the solar system to save the world. I love Ryland and Rocky, their chemistry worked so well together, making the space scenes fun and emotional. While on earth, Weir does this same sort of thing with Stratt and a few other characters that help add more humor and realism to the world. With an easy to read prose, and some musical note language Weir definitely made this accessible to all, even making sure the science was easy to understand. But Ray Porter’s narration is probably what makes this book 10 times better. My favorite thing about a narrator, is one who gets into their performance. It’s not just an intellectual reading of words, but a true performance that helps you feel the personality of the character but also the highs and lows of the situation. When Ryland was angry, sad, frustrated, happy or excited, Porter took you on that journey too. It’s only mid-March but this is easily y favorite read of 2026 so far. I highly, highly, highly, recommend reading or listening to this whether you see this review before or after the movie has come out. Project Hail Mary is going to take you on a journey with characters that you won’t soon forget.

review_title: My Thoughts on the Novel, Project Hail Mary…
body: I’m no fan of hard science fiction, mostly because the science (fiction) therein can befuddle me, and I’ll find myself rereading passages just to get the gist of things. This was the case for Project Hail Mary by Andy Weir, but the rest of the narrative is so well-written, accessible, and even heartwarming that, at times, the science did not matter. Essentially, the world is going to end, thanks to microscopic organisms that eat the sun. Yes, that sun, our sun. A multinational team comes together to create a project that utilizes these tiny organisms as fuel, enabling a team to travel across the universe to a different solar system where these entities pose no danger. The team is tasked with finding out the reasons behind this. Dr. Ryland Grace, a reluctant science teacher who named these entities after conducting research, is tricked—and that’s a mild way to describe what occurred to him—into joining the team and journeying light-years to the solar system in question. After some tragedy, he wakes up alone, with amnesia, to face the problem at hand. Soon Grace meets an alien. And the narrative rises above tropes and plot elements to become something much, much better. It is said that science fiction stories are mostly tales of humanity, and this is quite a glowing example of that contention. Alongside the developing relationship between Grace and the alien, the narrative is punctuated by flashbacks, providing background on the who, where, and why of the mission. With science and collaboration, Grace saves both the human race and an alien race, and even takes an unprecedented step to save a new friend. Another book by Andy Weir that was adapted into a film, The Martian, features a lone hero facing an impossible predicament. So when it comes to one man versus Nature (or science), Weir can truly weave a compelling tale. The same intent, style, and elements are included here, in Project Hail Mary. I eagerly await more books by this author. For fans of hard science fiction and of good stories, I highly recommend this book.

If I had one criticism, it would be that the minor characters in Hail Mary feel less fleshed out than the minor characters in Artemis and especially The Martian--I can still remember the conversations that Venkat Kapoor had with random people as they argued over trivial things like how many redundant radios there were on Mars. But the minor characters having less depth just makes the main characters feel even more fleshed out, so no complaints. As much as each book explores very niche areas of science, they also deal with larger themes. The Martian dealt with scientific problems handled by all of Earth and was about all the things that could go wrong trying to save one man on a harsh planet. Artemis was very plot-driven and focused on one person overcoming many obstacles while circumventing a very intricate city on the moon, the specific rules and building blocks of the city creating very unusual scenarios that had to be dealt with. (Slight spoiler?) Hail Mary is about two people and how they work together to solve a problem that will destroy their species. It is easy to feel like the main characters in the other two books are alone (at least part of the time) because of how they solve problems and the obstacles they must face, but this one feels so different because it is about friendship and facing  obstacles together. This fascinating relationship fuels the entire story, and I wish it kept going just so I can see more moments of them being friends. I can't recommend this enough. If you liked The Martian, there is no way you won't feel the same about Hail Mary. And if you don't like The Martian, it's because you haven't read it yet, in which case, read that too!

body: Project Hail Mary is an absolute masterpiece of hard sci-fi. Andy Weir does it again — this book is every bit as gripping and clever as The Martian, but with even higher stakes. The story follows Ryland Grace, who wakes up alone on a spaceship with no memory of how he got there or why he’s on a desperate mission light-years from Earth. What follows is a brilliant blend of problem-solving, scientific ingenuity, and heartfelt moments that had me completely hooked from the first page. Weir’s greatest strength is making complex science feel accessible and exciting. You’ll learn real physics, biology, and astronomy while cheering for characters that feel incredibly real (yes, even the non-human ones). The twists are perfectly timed, the tension is relentless, and the ending is deeply satisfying. If you love smart, optimistic sci-fi with humor, heart, and “one more chapter” energy, this is essential reading. Easily one of my favorite books of the last few years. Highly recommended — 5/5 stars.

review_title: Wake up and smell the terrestrial crisis!
body: Many people can relate to the experience of waking up and having a Jumanji-esque "what year is it" existential crisis - which of course is usually in jest, or quickly passes. For Ryland Grace, waking up is an altogether cataclysmic experience - he can't remember his own name, or what he's supposed to be doing, or why there's two corpses and a robot in the room with him. With time, his memory's return in the hazy way a dandelion's seeds float on the wind - and he's slowly reacquainted with the impossible nature of his task. Alone and hurtling through deep space on a veritable chimera of a ship fueled by every government agency on the planet, he's humanity's last hope against an extinction-level event taking place back at home. And with the unexpected help of an ally, the odds may just be in his favor. I walked into this book fairly blind - it was my book club's choice ahead of the movie adaptation coming out this year, and I missed out on "The Martian" when it was popular, so I was pleasantly surprised with how much fun (and anxiety) I had while reading about Ryland Grace (main character name if I ever saw one) and his schoolteacher smarts fighting it out at the brink of the universe. The book did a good job in slow-baking a lot of nebulous concepts into something the average reader could parse out and enjoy, which I think can be difficult for science fiction books - and while I doubt much of the science will stand up to proper scrutiny, this isn't one of those books that's diving into realism. You're here to have fun, and maybe review some of what you've forgotten from high school or entry-level college courses, and that's okay. I think the book did a great job in capturing the desperation of what the internet cryptids would call an "XK Class End-Of-The-World Scenario" and took a good stab in imagining what that might look like from a world government/cooperation standpoint, if with heavy liberties towards how maturely some world leaders would act. I think the humanistic and scientific facets of the mission, which was revealed in piecemeal as Grace's memory catches up, worked really well from a pacing and storytelling perspective, and while there were loose ends I really wanted follow-up on that were never tied up properly, I don't think this necessarily ruined my enjoyment of the story overall. I'll be looking forward to seeing how this one plays out on the big screen since there's a lot of internalization and explanation from a reader standpoint, but overall I'd be up to reading more Andy Weir stories in the future.

product_title: Project Hail Mary
body: I consider The Martian my favorite fictional novel of the last 15-20 years. The movie was incredible in that they actually followed the book closer than 99% of other films based on books. It remains my favorite movie of the last 15 years or so as well. I don't know anyone (personally) that loves either of them as much as I do. With that said, I was REALLY looking forward to Artemis. It was good...but, it was certainly not in the same caliber as The Martian was (at least not for me). I enjoyed it a lot, however and appreciated how author Andy Weir chose to go in a completely different direction and not just rehash another similar story, which I am certain would have been great as well. As a result, I was cautious regarding Project Hail Mary. It sounded a little too close to The Martian, but yet, also different in that the circumstances simply could not be more opposite and the stakes so much higher. I'm trying to figure out the best way to summarize without giving too much away from this utterly compelling novel. As I read several reviews, I noticed a recurring theme: SCIENCE. Lots and LOTS of science. Holy cow, they were right. Many years ago I read Apollo 13 and Jim Lovell and his co-writer, try as they might, simply could not dumb down Orbital Mechanics anywhere near enough for me to have even a minor clue as to what they were attempting to say...I just skipped 90% of it and hoped that the sentences written afterwards, would help to make sense of what I had just skimmed over. I'm a lot of things, but a math wizard is definitely not one of them. Michael Crichton (Jurassic Park) had an amazing talent for dumbing-down the science of what he was trying to explain in ways that genuinely made sense (most of the time). Not everyone has this talent, and I would say Andy Weir falls squarely in between. He's certainly better than Jim Lovell, but not quite as good as Crichton. But then again, outside of a science textbook, I haven't really read anything with quite as MUCH science as Project Hail Mary. So maybe he's just as good, but he just puts more science into his books than Crichton, maybe that's it...? Either way, be prepared for a lot of astonishingly interesting science within the pages of this novel...and I DO mean a LOT. I don't say this to make you wary or steer you away...on the contrary, Andy Weir has a special talent for making hard science truly entertaining. The book opens with an absolutely amazing and frightening premise: an astronaut awakes from an induced coma to find the only other two people on board have died at some point along their journey...but it gets worse. He has no idea who he is, or why he's on the ship, and oh yeah, they look to be a long way from home. A really, REALLY long way from home. In fact, the sun he sees isn't actually OUR sun at all. He's managed to leave our solar system entirely. And he has no idea why. ((Minor Spoilers)) The book goes through some clever flash-backs, which set the stage for why the mission happens, and slowly, carefully explains how they managed to get so far away from earth in such a short amount of time. Basically, earth's sun seems to be dying. At the rate of decay, we have maybe 19 years left before the gradual cooling has catastrophic consequences resulting in the death of billions (best guess). Why the sun is dimming is quite the conundrum in the first place. Turns out it really isn't dying, it's being killed by an outside source...which turns out to be easily the greatest find in history. It's alien life, and they are using the sun for food, essentially. It's alien life, but not intelligent life. But still, wow! ALIENS, right??? After this monumental discovery, and some tremendous research done by the most improbable scientist, the investigation into what is happening and why and what to do about it expands exponentially to other nations in order to pool all the resources possible to hopefully save the sun, and by extension, the human race as well. They learn. A LOT. A plan is put together, and with the help of the newly discovered microscopic alien life, which can also double as a power source (along with a few other nifty surprises), they begin to create one last, Hail Mary that could very well be the last chance we might have to save earth. It's audacious. It's dangerous, and it is absolutely critical that it succeed. As our astronaut's memory slowly unravels, so does his identity: Ryland Grace. He's a teacher on earth. Just a science teacher. Not even a college professor. He's amazingly smart, though. But he's no astronaut...and certainly not one who would volunteer to go on a one-way mission to another solar system to "try" and save humanity. Yet here he is. Alone. light years from earth, trying to solve the biggest riddle in all of human history. Ryland accepts his situation, such as it is, with relative indifference (for the most part). It doesn't matter HOW he got here. He's here now and he may as well use that time to be as productive as possible, right? Along the way, he unravels even more information regarding the microscopic alien life which is slowly dimming our sun during some additional flashbacks. The aliens, dubbed, "Astrophage" are quite the galactic plague as it turns out. Stars all over the galaxy are also losing their light, all due to the little buggers. All that is, except one particular star named, Tau Ceti. Now why would that one star be unaffected by Astrophage, when every single star around it has been affected to some degree. The plan is to go there and figure it out and send the information back, hopefully in time to save the sun before the damage to earth is beyond repair. There is an incredible amount of stuff going on. The story switches from Tau Ceti to flashbacks of how the whole mission was planned and implemented (which is VERY entertaining, especially Director Stratt, who may actually be my favorite character in the entire novel). Weir is becoming quite adept at building tension, and abruptly switching the story from Tau Ceti back to earth and building more of the backstory then switching back to Tau Ceti. Keeping it all in check and most importantly, interesting all while mixing in a healthy dose of science, which I am to understand is pretty much all genuine, is quite the juggling act. I have long known science can be astronomically entertaining (see what I did there?) when done right...but unfortunately very few people in a position to teach science actually know the best way to create that interest in others. I can say without reservation, Andy Weir definitely knows how to do it...at least in written form. There is so much I want to say more regarding this truly phenomenal story, but I simply cannot without ruining a lot of the fun and surprises revealed along the way...and it is killing me to keep it locked in. Though I labeled a spoiler warning earlier, I don't think it gave away any more than what the author himself has revealed in interviews he has done regarding the book, and what you can glean from reading the summary here and just a couple other reviews. Tying all of that science together is truly astonishing to me. The creativity to put it into a novel that is remarkably exciting to read is nothing more than incredible talent. Kudo's to Andy Weir for not just hitting a home run, Project Hail Mary is a Grand Slam all the way. I truly did not want this story to end. By the way, I enjoyed the ending quite a bit. I don't know if everyone will. But it was fine for me. I think the ending screams "sequel" at some point too. A lot was left open-ended (IMO) and I wouldn't mind reading a follow-up to this. It doesn't HAVE to happen, but there are a lot of ways where the story could go if Andy chose to do it. Just sayin'. Just run out and buy this book.

product_title: Project Hail Mary
body: I realize that Project Hail Mary already has approximately the population of a small city reviewing it, but I loved this book so much that I want to add my five stars to the pile. Andy Weir had me at the science. Actually, he had me at spectroscopy. I'm a spectroscopist, and discovering that spectroscopy isn't merely mentioned in this novel but plays an important role in understanding what is happening was ridiculously satisfying. More broadly, I loved the way Weir uses science throughout the book. It isn't decoration applied to make the story sound technical. The characters observe, hypothesize, calculate, experiment, get things wrong, revise their hypotheses, and try again. Science is how the story moves forward. And, remarkably, Weir makes all of that tremendous fun. The human protagonist is smart without being implausibly infallible. He has flashes of ingenuity and moments of spectacularly ordinary human fallibility. He can be noble and deeply flawed—and, importantly, is capable of being dismayed by his own flaws. That makes him much more interesting than a conventional heroic scientist who always knows what to do. Then there's Rocky. What a wonderful creation. Weir makes his alien just human enough that we can form an emotional connection with him, while keeping him sufficiently non-human that we never forget we're encountering a genuinely different life-form. The differences aren't merely cosmetic. Biology, perception, environment, language, technology, and ways of thinking all matter. And somehow, across all those differences, a friendship develops. By the time that relationship is fully established, Project Hail Mary has quietly become one of the best buddy stories I've read. Two intelligent beings who shouldn't even be able to communicate gradually learn not only how to work together, but how to understand, trust, tease, worry about, and care for one another. That's where the book becomes more than a clever science-fiction adventure. Rocky raises fascinating questions about which qualities we think of as "human" that might actually be something more universal: curiosity, loyalty, humor, cooperation, friendship, even love. Speaking of humor: this book is genuinely funny. Sometimes wry, sometimes absurd, and occasionally laugh-out-loud funny. I know this because I read part of it on an airplane and actually laughed out loud. Fortunately, the person sitting next to me was wearing headphones, so my dignity remained largely intact. I loved the adventure. I loved the friendship. I loved the imperfect protagonist. And I absolutely loved encountering a science-fiction novel in which the science is not simply scenery but an essential part of the story. Five enthusiastic stars. Did I mention the spectroscopy? For readers who enjoy: The Martian, also by Andy Weir, Contact by Carl Sagan, and The Mote in God's Eye by Larry Niven and Jerry Pournelle—science fiction in which figuring out the science is part of the adventure, and encountering something truly alien gives us a new way of looking at ourselves. Cocktail pairing: A Moscow Mule — vodka, ginger beer, and lime. Vodka gets its small but memorable nod in the novel, while the copper mug seems entirely appropriate for a book in which materials, chemistry, engineering, and the physical properties of practically everything can suddenly become important. Besides, after spending several hundred pages trying to save humanity using astrophysics, biology, engineering, chemistry—and, yes, spectroscopy—you've earned a drink. Just analyze its spectrum before consuming. For science, and, ya know, just in case...

product_title: Project Hail Mary
body: In American football, a hail mary is a very long pass typically made in desperation and with a very small chance of achieving completion. The term carries a reference to the Catholic prayer exactly because of its difficulty to succeed. Andy Weir probably had this sports reference in mind when he chose the name of the space mission depicted in his book, but in a podcast with Neil deGrasse Tyson he confessed he is also guilty of choosing 'Grace' as the last name of his main character, which, of course, circles back to the prayer (Ave Maria, gratia plena.) The word grace, Northrop Frye writes, is a most important thematic word in Shakespearean comedy, and it seems a magical coincidence that I've been studying As You Like It while also reading PHM, because I think I've found an unexpected connection between these two otherwise completely unrelated texts, and I should say that it is not only because there is a De Boys family in AYLI and a DuBois in PHM**. The thing that made me really like Andy Weir's The Martian more than 5 years ago was that Mark Watney--the sci fi novel's hero--never really became depressed or extremely frustrated to make the book heavy and dark : no matter how hard the challenges faced by him in the hostile environment of Mars were, Watney was always able to find a positive angle to avoid falling apart--it is not that he was naively optimistic but rather that he remained focused even when the odds were against him. That is what Ryland Grace in PHM, the biophysicist turned into high school teacher turned into the only hope to save planet Earth, also represents--in a mission that otherwise would be as gloomy as literally the end of the world. This feel-good vibe that permeates Weir's books is also present in AYLI--no matter how dangerous or urgent the situation may be, there is a permanent sense that wit and competence will prevail over conflict and corruption and that goodness eventually will find its way to reward the characters, and readers and audience alike. Odd as it may sound, underneath the sci fi plot there is a pastoral quality in PHM. In the end, space is an isolated and a socially protected setting where characters may well seek redemption without being affected by corruption, vice and malice of the society of the 'normal world'. Ryland Grace wakes up from amnesia in a spaceship, which distinctly contrasts with the iron fist of Eva Stratt as project manager to save Earth from apocalypse, just like the Forest of Arden contrasts with the life of the court of Duke Frederick, from which Rosalind is unjustly banished. Northrop Frye even has a name for this realm where the pastoral characters are transformed from the 'normal' to an 'ideal' : green world, which has analogies not only to the fertile world of ritual but to the dream world created out of desires. In Shakespeare, this realm is not an escape from reality but a genuine form of the world that human life tries to imitate. When life is transformed inside the green world--and so gets closer to the ideal the reader and the audience also aspire to--there comes the reward. It is as if that graceful hail mary long shot, difficult and unlikely as it may have been in the beginning, finally comes home at the end. That is the generosity Shakespeare adds to Rosalind's epilogue, when she invites women and men to enjoy the play as they like it, and that is Weir's generosity in keeping our hearts warm even far away, orbiting another star.

body: August 2025, review written in 2026: I listened to this on an 11-hour car trip (there and back) and it was the perfect listen. Because the narration was unfamiliar to me and I hadn’t read it in 4 years, I initially thought I hadn’t read this book before and it took certain key moments for me to realize I had actually read this book. I realize now that I’ve read my past review that I thought this book would be just as good either way (reading on your own or listening to the audio) and I was right. In many ways, it was a different experience, but Ray Porter made it a great experience and absolutely made the miles pass by very easily. So I highly recommend the audio! That said, the movie has now come out and everyone is telling me to go see it, both people who have read the book and people who have not. I love Ryan Gosling, so I am looking forward to it! November 2021: I really enjoyed this one! Unlike “the Martian” which I think was even better when listened to, this one I read myself and I think it would be fine either way. Considering how much I loved The Martian (it was better than the movie), I knew it would be a hard sell to like this one as much. But about a quarter of the way in there’s a plot twist (no spoilers) that did it for me! In this one, Ryland ends up alone in space far from home and he has to figure out how to save not just himself, but all of humanity. He’s a trained microbiologist and junior high science teacher, but when he wakes up at the beginning, he doesn’t remember anything or where he is. I love how he slowly regains his memories through flashes to the past that explains things, but also how these memories slowly help him address the problem at hand. At times convenient, in terms of the coincidences, I still love how the story unfolded. For those of you who were offended by the language in the first book, there were no such issues in this one. I wouldn’t have minded either way, but perhaps this could be read by a younger audience without parents getting upset about the language. But seriously, have you heard how middle school students talk when they think you’re not listening? I love how Andy Weir included discussions of global warming and how it could be used to help in their situation. But I also like how he did his best to talk about the ramifications of anything the scientists in this book did. The ending was absolutely satisfying and I’ll leave it at that as I think this book is better read without any preknowledge. Overall, I loved it at least as much as The Martian, but for different reasons. While physical science was definitely discussed, Ryland was a microbiologist so there was a lot of discussion about life and what life needs to grow and duplicate, etc. I’ve been helping students recently with biology, so much of the discussion was coincidentally relevant!

product_title: The Women: A Novel
body: America has always portrayed itself as a country of advanced thinking, but the truth under its boasting is that , for the most part,  if women were a reason to be proud, America ignored them.  Hannah reveals this "critical gender theory" in her book about a nurse serving in Vietnam. Her main character is Frankie McGrath , a young woman  who becomes an Army nurse in Vietnam. She believes she should serve her country in some way  after her brother is killed in the war shortly after he enlists.  She is hoping her mother and most importantly, her father will be proud of her. She gets the exact opposite reaction. They expected her to get married and have children.  Her father has a "hero's wall" of family members who served in  past wars. She can only be on that wall after she gets married, and the picture is her wedding picture, and it will be the only picture of her.  The wall is symbolic of what society deemed  was heroic  and only men could be heroic in that way.  There was only room for a woman if  she married, became a housewife, and had children. While this choice is perfectly  acceptable, it should not be perfectly binding as the only way for a woman to show her worth.  Frankie is sure she belongs on that wall as a nurse who serves in  the Army. Her parents disagree and tell their friends , when Frankie goes off to the war, thst she is studying abroad.  But it isn't just her family whose narrow vision of Frankie affects her life.  The Army itself has allowed societal rules to dictate how women are treated. Getting to Vietnam is no picnic for Frankie. While her fellow travelers are all men dressed in comfortable fatigues, she must travel in her blouse, tight green jacket, narrow, skirt, nylons held up by a regulation girdle (despite panty hose being available) , and heels.  The life of a nurse in a war zone is dangerous, frightening, and traumatic.  The war makes less and less sense to Frankie as she stuffs vital organs back into shredded chests and abdominal cavities, and helps doctors amputate more than one limb per patient. Frankie comes to realize  with growing horror what is really going on in Vietnam, that America was losing that war, but didn't mind sacrificing more and more young men so that the government could save face.  It is a rude awakening for her. When she returns home after two tours of duty, she is treated with disrespect by the public, the VA, and her parents. The country had been told that no women went to Vietnam, so Frankie could not have been there even though she so obviously was. That has always been the problem with woman who don't follow the rules society dictates. If they insist on showing how wrong headed that thinking is, society will just have to minimize them if not ignore them.  Suffering from what is now  recognized as PTSD, Frankie hits rock bottom before she is able, with the help of her nurse friends who also served, to find a way to survive.  The Vietnam protests by the veterans themselves as well as everyone else who  raised their voices,  finally ended the war.  Eventually, the government admitted that over 6,000 nurses,most of them women,  served in Vietnam.  Hannah's story is thoroughly researched.  Her depiction of war torn Vietnam is riveting.  One turns the pages to end the war as soon as possible.  Frankie's struggles with  the war and at home are realistic, heartbreaking,  and deeply troubling, but they don't destroy her.  She survived Vietnam, and she survives coming back home.
